topics.title: k The Art of Guessing
topics.text:
Hello, it is I, brainpopper, who is about to present to you the most valuable piece of knowledge you will have ever read. 







[center]THE ART OF GUESSING

Applicable to MATHCOUNTS Competitions[/center]



Being more than 3 years into MATHCOUNTS competitions, I have acquired a large amount of experience through practice and testing. Now, have you ever been in a situation where you have little time left to do a few problems? Do not worry, For I have a top secret method to guessing ANY answer on ANY problem. Now, keep in mind, I have studied this intense topic for many years and have gained multiple PhD's and other doctorates in this field and I trust you to keep this information secret.



Now, first of all, we must analyze the problem itself. What type of problem is (Algebra, probability and counting, geometry, number sense, etc.), and what must your answer be expressed in (A common fraction, mixed number, decimal rounded to the nearest x, whole number, etc.)?



Let us begin with the rules!







[center]ALGEBRA[/center]





1.) If the question has a variable $x$ raised to a large power or such (i.e. $x^{10} - x^6$), the answer will usually be a multiple of $50$.



2.) If the answer shall be expressed as a common fraction in lowest terms, the denominator shall always be prime, and the numerator shall be prime, a multiple of $5$, a multiple or $7$, or a multiple of $3$. (i.e. $7/2$)



3.) If the answer shall be expressed as a mixed number, just give up. It's not like any problems even need to be expressed as a mixed number anyways.



4.) If the answer shall be expressed as a decimal rounded to the nearest $x$, the value of the decimal part $x$ will usually be more than $20$ unless it's a money problem. If it's a money problem, it's fair game. (i.e.$7.21$, $8.50$, $15.75$, $\$2.15$)



5.) If the answer  shall be expressed as a whole number, it is usually a multiple of $6$, a multiple of $21$, a prime number, $4$ (the number), or $24$ (the number).



6.) If the problem contains many complex polynomials and exponents ($4x^4 + 3x - 71 + y^2 - 3y^8$ etc.), the answer is probably $1$ or $0$.







[center]PROBABILITY AND COUNTING[/center]



dont take this section seriously



1.) If the answer shall be expressed as a whole number, take the largest number in the problem (i.e. $1005$) and add it to the sum of its digits. ($1005 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 5 = 1011$)



2.) If the answer shall be expressed as a fraction, take the units digit of the problem number ($5 \rightarrow 5, 23 \rightarrow 3$), slap it into the numerator, and put a prime number in the denominator, preferably one less than 2 times the numerator, although you can use all prime numbers less than $13$. ($5/7, 5/11, 3/5, 3/7$)







[center]NUMBER THEORY[/center]





1.) The answer is probably $24$.







[center]GEOMETRY[/center]





1.) If the answer shall be expressed as a common fraction, it is probably in the form of $\frac{x^2}{y^2}$



2.) If you ever get stuck calculating the lengths of a geometrical figure, just take some lead from your mechanical pencil (or your friend's) and break it into a few "unit leads". You can use these to relatively measure the side lengths. MATHCOUNTS says that their drawings are not to scale, but they ARE.



3.) If the answer shall be expressed as a radical in simplest terms, it's most likely going to be a prime number in the radical and an even number, a multiple of $3$, or the numbers $5$ or $7$ as the multiplier of the radical. If it needs to be a fraction as well, it'll probably be a prime number in the denominator or of the form $\frac{x\sqrt{y}}{x-1}$ or the other way around.









So that was it for now. Hopefully you learned something from this. Good luck on your tests!

P.S. should I make a vol. 2?

The following mathematical expression is incomplete:

$$2\,\_\_\,2\,\_\_\,2\,\_\_\,\cdots\,\_\_\,2\,\_\_\,2$$There are $2018$ twos in the expression above, and $2017$ missing operations. Each blank is to be filled with either a plus sign, a minus sign, times, or divide.

topics.title: Integer Sequences
topics.text:
A sequence of positive integers is defined by the following:

If the current term is divisible by 3, the next term is generated by dividing the curent term by 3.

If the current term is not divisible by 3, the next term is generated by subtrating the current term by 1.

If the first term of the sequence is a 3 digit number, and the 6th term is 1, what is the sum of all possible first terms?

topics.title: A trivial necklace problem
topics.text:
A while ago at Math class, we were discussing about combinatorics. One of the questions was as follows:



"How many ways are there to arrange 3 red beads, 5 blue beads, 4 green beads and 3 white beads on a necklace, such that all the beads of the same color are together?"



My answer was 6, because it was just simply the number of circular permutations of 4 objects. $\frac{4!}4=6$.



However, my teacher said it was incorrect. He/she thinks that the answer is 24, because according to him/her, you don't count the rotations.



What should be the correct answer?

topics.title: Maryland Mathalon Rant
topics.text:
Here is a rant on today's Mathalon, a local Maryland math competition. This isn't a formal essay of any sort but just me ranting, so prepare for low quality.



Alright, let me start off by saying that the Mathalon is probably the lowest quality math competition (in terms of problems' quality) in existence, perhaps save for the MCPS Math Meets. All the problems on the Individual Round were literally trivial common core math, and the hardest problems on it were probably easier than a Mathcounts School Sprint #30.



Not only that, but the director of the competition or whoever that was (that NSA dude) should, in my opinion, just stay away from math competitions. Not to say that he's a bad person or anything, but he really doesn't understand how math contests work.



For example, one of the problems was "Find the 12th number in the sequence: 2, 9, 28...."

There are actually an infinite amount of answers to this problem- no matter what number you say the 12th term is, there'll be some sort of sequence. Don't get me wrong, I'm normally fine with this kind of non-rigorous "pattern-style" problems, but I'm not fine when there are only three terms. If there were like 5 or 6 terms, then common sense would dictate that it's $n^3+1$, but in this problem, there's simply not enough terms for common sense to dictate anything.



And when one of the kids came up and told this to the director, the director basically said "Oh, but you have to choose the best answer- because all the other ones will give complicated sequences, but $n^3+1$ is simple".

My first reaction to that statement was, "Are you actually stupid?" and my second reaction was "Yes, you actually are." If you write such a terrible problem, then at least admit that it's a terrible and ambiguous problem, even if you mark the non-1729 answers as wrong.



Another thing was that the tiebreaks system was absolute garbage. Basically, there were 30 questions on the individual round, and then 2 tiebreak questions at the end. As expected, I breezed through the 30 questions and the first tiebreaker easily, and then there was quite a bit of time left for me to work on the second tiebreaker, which was literally the worst problem I've ever seen. It was basically a classic logic riddle (the "Heaven or Hell Puzzle", except the "flavor text" was different), literally copied verbatim from the internet except with an extra component that doesn't really affect the answer. Again, don't get me wrong, I'm fine with these non-standard types of questions, but I'm not fine with problems copied from the internet, especially when it's a "classic".



Now where was I again? Oh, yes, tiebreakers. I ended up somehow not making any sillies and getting the first 30 questions and tiebreaker 1 correct, placing second individually. I originally had thought that the first place finisher answered the second tiebreaker right and I didn't, but it turned out that he didn't get it either; we both answered the exact same questions, yet he got first and I got second. How could that be? Well, it turned out that the other kid "showed better work" on the tiebreaker 1, which I still don't see how can be possible- my work was a clear, simple, and concise (and, of course, correct) half-liner, which really can't be disputed as "unelegant" or "bashy".



In my puzzlement, I read the Individual Round instructions again, and it said that the graders would grade tiebreakers based on "everything including but not limited to spelling, neatness, conciseness, and of course correctness." This is stupidity at its finest. Math solutions should be graded on correctness and perhaps elegance, but certainly not such subjective criteria.



I could go on for another ten thousand words about everything else messed up about the Mathalon, but I've already spent nearly half an hour writing this, much longer than I expected. The point? The Mathalon is a trash competition, and, I suspect, so are many similar local competitions. If these kinds of contests are most students' first impressions of math competitions (as they indeed are), then is there any wonder that less and less people are participating in math contests?

topics.title: k AMC 8 Tips and Tricks
topics.text:
Hello, I am going into 7th grade. I would like to give out some tips and tricks that I have to others taking the test for their first time (or maybe need a few tips). I got a 21 on the 2017 AMC 8. If you disagree with what I say, please do so nicely, so that this doesn't start a flame war. I hope that this will help a lot of people on the 2018 AMC 8, and hopefully increase their score

AMC 8 Tips and Tricks1. Don't be nervous.The day before the test, get a good night sleep so that you aren't sleepy during the test. Also, make sure that you don't get nervous during the test because when you are nervous, you will most likely do worse in the test. Remember, the AMC's don't have that much of an impact. What you really need to learn from the AMC is to have fun and try your best.




2. Bring the materials needed for the test.The last time I took the test, I forgot to bring a ruler, graph paper, and an eraser. Because I didn't bring graph paper, I had very limited work, and used mental math on some of the last few problems (causing me to miss #22). Also, make sure that you get your "business" done before the test, so that you don't have headaches or uncomfort during the test.




3. What to do if you don't know the answers to a problemIf you don't know the answer to the last few problems (or the ones before), just guess. Remember, there is no guessing penalty!




4. What to prepare for in the testOn the test, there is usually 2 geometry problems in the last 5 problems, so make sure you prepare for some geometry problems. Also, there are usually lots of word problems and easy calculations in the first 15 - 20 problems. There is also usually 1 or 2 counting and probability problems in each test, and around 3 - 8 algebra problems in each test




5. Tips to what to do in time pressureWhen there is close to a minute left and you don't know the answer to more than 3 problems, try to do as much as you can. In the last 10-20 seconds, just guess the problems that you don't know, because that always gives you a better chance than if you don't answer it at all.




6. Keeping track of timeRemember to look at the time on the clock as you start. AMC 8's are 40 minutes. Keep track of how many minutes you have left, and when you have less than 10 minutes, don't worry. Do as much as you can. If you have a watch, you should bring it, as when I took the test, the clock in the room didn't work.




7. Write clearlyWriting clearly cost me a whole point on the test. On one of the problems, I wrote a 6, and it looked like a 0, so I ended up getting a totally different answer. Writing clearly will usually reduce some mistakes done in the test.




8. Double check (if you can)Double check if you are done before 40 minutes are up. You can mark the questions that you need to double check so that you can come back to it, so that you don't need to double check the questions that you are super confident about. If you have enough time to check all of the questions, make sure you do because you might have made a small addition error or a small subtraction error.

topics.title: Micro Battles
topics.text:
NikoIsLife has recently found a game from the App Store, called Micro Battles, a mobile game meant to be played by two players. The game has four different minigames available to be played.



However, one thing annoys NikoIsLife.





[center]IMAGE[/center]



NikoIsLife only downloaded the Trial version of Micro Battles. Which means, the game will randomly choose one type of minigame out of the four, and that is the only minigame NikoIsLife can play for the whole day. (Each minigame has an equal chance of being chosen.)



But, NikoIsLife is clever. He/she knows that he/she can just keep on uninstalling the app and install it again, and the game would randomly choose a minigame again. NikoIsLife keeps on doing this until he/she gets to play all the minigames.



If NikoIsLife does this, what is the average number of uninstalls/installs needed in order to have played all the minigames of Micro Battles?

topics.text:
Hello these are some geometry questions from a local math competition :)

I know the solutions to half of them I just want to see your method of solving them

Thanks!

Please provide Solutions quickly.



1. The medians to the legs of a right triangle have lengths $10$ and 4$\sqrt{10}$. Find the length of the triangle's hypotenuse. (Solved)

2. The sides of a right triangle measure $5x$, $4x+13$, and $x-1$. If $x$ is an integer, find the sum of the digits of $x$. (Solved)

3. In triangle $ABC$, $AB=5$, $BC=16$, $AC=\sqrt{153}$ and $D$ is on segment $BC$. Compute the sum of all possible integral values of $AD$. (Solved)

4. Right triangle $ABC$ has hypotenuse $AC$, angle $CAB=30^\circ$, and $BC=\sqrt{2}$. Right triangle $ACD$ has hypotenuse $AD$ and angle $DAC=45^\circ$. The interiors of $ABC$ and $ACD$ do not overlap. Find the length of the perpendicular from $D$ onto $AB$.  (Solved)

5. A circle with center $O$ has a radius of $5$ while a circle with center $A$ has a radius of $13$. Given that $OA=26$, what is the sum of the lengths of one common external and one common internal tangent between the two circles.

6. Triangle $ABC$, is inscribed in a circle with center $X$, when $\angle{ABC}=90^\circ$, $BC=18$, and $AB=80$. The altitude from point $B$ intersects $AC$ at point $D$. What is the distance between point $X$ and point $D$. (Solved)

7. In triangle, $ABC$, $AB=7$, $BC=8$, and $\angle{ABC}=60^\circ$. What is the length of $AC$.

8. Find the total surface area of a regular dodecahedron with side length $10$.

9.  What is the shortest distance from point $(3,4)$ and equation $x^2+y^2-42x-20y=-505$.

10. What is the volume of a tetrahedron with height $2\sqrt{3}$.

11. What is the difference between the areas of an inscribed regular hexagon and octagon in a circle with radius $1$.

12. Imagine a $12$ by $16$ piece of paper is folded along its diagonal. What is the region of overlap (The region where paper is on the top). Please provide diagram. (Solved)

13. Imagine going from point $(0,0)$ to $(3,4)$ to $(14,7)$ to $(24,10)$ to $(26,17)$. Given that you can only travel up or to the right $1$ unit at a time. What are the last $2$ digits of the total number of possible paths for the entire trip. Consider this problem on a standard Cartesian Plane.

14. How do you find the surface area and volume of a torus.

15. A ninja named Ninju is standing $5$ miles north of a perfectly straight river. He wants to get to a dojo $10$ miles east and $5$ miles north of his current location. However, he is very thirsty, and wants to stop by the river first for a drink of water. What is the shortest distance Ninju can travel if he wants to stop by the river before heading to the dojo?

16.  Consider a convex quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals AC and BD that are perpendicular to one another. Given

that the quadrilateral has side lengths AB = 21, BC = 26, and CD = 32, what is the length of side AD?

Suppose there are two distinct points $P_1$ and $P_2$ in the coordinate plane, entirely contained within the square of side length $2$ with vertices in the set $\{ (1,1), (1,-1), (-1,-1), (-1,1)\}$, such that $a$ is the length of $\overline{P_1 P_2}$ and $b$ is the sum of the $y$-coordinates of the two points. Two new, but also distinct, points $P_3$ and $P_4$ are plotted in the plane such that the difference in their $y$-coordinates is $a$ and the difference in their $x$-coordinates is $b$. Armed with this information, what is the greatest integer less than or equal to the maximum possible length of $\overline{P_3 P_4}$?

Let $\ell$ be the least common multiple of two distinct integers between $1$ and $100$ (inclusive), and let $g$ be their greatest common divisor. What is the maximum possible value of the greatest integer less than or equal to $\frac{\ell g + \ell + g}{\ell^2 + g^2}$?

topics.title: 9 Should we have an elementary school math forum?
topics.text:
I think we should have an elementary school math forum because of a good bit of users that are at or below 6th grade. As I have heard, some users are as young as 9. Also, some of the problems in the MSM forum seem way to easy for "middle school math", for instance, this one: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h1683848_calender_problem

And also this one:

https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h1683327_this_is_sparta_2

Maybe it's just me that thinks these are too easy, but what do you guys think? Should we have "elementary school math" or not?
